content: Drug interaction studies indicate that interactions with inhibitors of liver enzymes are not expected because olopatadine is primarily eliminated through renal excretion. In vitro studies demonstrated that olopatadine does not inhibit the metabolism of specific substrates for CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, or CYP3A4. Based on these findings, drug interactions involving P450 enzyme inhibition are unlikely. Additionally, due to the modest protein binding of olopatadine (approximately 55%), drug interactions caused by displacement from plasma proteins are also not anticipated. Nonclinical toxicology studies showed that oral administration of olopatadine was not carcinogenic in mice and rats at doses up to 500 mg/kg/day and 200 mg/kg/day, respectively. These doses correspond to approximately 420 and 340 times the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) for adults and adolescents aged 12 years and older, and 500 and 400 times the MRHD for children aged 6–11 years, based on a mg/m² basis for intranasal administration. Genotoxicity studies, including an in vitro bacterial reverse mutation test (Ames test), an in vitro mammalian chromosome aberration assay, and an in vivo mouse micronucleus test, revealed no evidence of genotoxicity. In fertility studies, oral administration of olopatadine to male and female rats at a dose of 400 mg/kg/day (approximately 680 times the MRHD for adults on a mg/m² basis) resulted in a decrease in the fertility index and reduced implantation rates. However, no effects on fertility were observed at a dose of 50 mg/kg/day (approximately 85 times the MRHD for adults on a mg/m² basis). Reproductive toxicology studies demonstrated that olopatadine was not teratogenic in rabbits and rats at oral doses up to 400 mg/kg/day and 600 mg/kg/day, respectively. These doses correspond to approximately 1,400 and 1,000 times the MRHD for adults on a mg/m² basis. However, a reduction in the number of live fetuses was observed in rabbits at oral doses of 25 mg/kg/day (approximately 88 times the MRHD for adults on a mg/m² basis) and higher, and in rats at oral doses of 60 mg/kg/day (approximately 100 times the MRHD for adults on a mg/m² basis) and higher. In rats, pup viability and body weights were reduced on day 4 postpartum at oral doses of 60 mg/kg/day (approximately 100 times the MRHD for adults on a mg/m² basis) and higher. No effects on pup viability were observed at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day (approximately 35 times the MRHD for adults on a mg/m² basis). Clinical studies evaluating the efficacy and safety of PATANASE Nasal Spray were conducted in three randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, multicenter, placebo-controlled trials lasting two weeks. These studies included adult and adolescent patients aged 12 years and older with symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinitis. The trials, conducted in the United States, involved 1,598 patients (556 males and 1,042 females). Of these, 1,005 patients were treated with PATANASE Nasal Spray, and 593 patients received a vehicle nasal spray as a placebo. Efficacy was assessed based on patient-reported severity of four individual nasal symptoms: nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, itchy nose, and sneezing. Symptom severity was recorded on a categorical scale ranging from 0 to 3 (0 = absent, 1 = mild, 2 = moderate, 3 = severe) as either reflective or instantaneous scores. Reflective scoring required patients to record symptom severity over the previous 12 hours, while instantaneous scoring required patients to record symptom severity at the time of assessment.
